newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak says skipping summit because of Israel.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak says skipping summit because of Israel.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Tuesday he was staying away from an emergency Middle East peace summit in Washington because he was displeased with Israel's attitude and actions towards the Palestinians.

"Our absence does give an indication that we are not pleased with the situation and obstinate acts of Israel concerning the Palestinians," Mubarak told reporters before he inaugurated a new line of the Cairo underground.

U.S. President Bill Clinton called the meeting to salvage the Middle East peace process after Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem last week touched off Israeli-Palestinian clashes that killed 72 Arabs and Jews.
Jordan's King Hussein, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat arrived in Washington for the summit, planned to start later on Tuesday.

The tunnel's opening has drawn international condemnation but Netnayahu, who is procrastinating on several peace pledges initiated by the former Labour government, has vowed Israel would keep it open forever.

"The statements that came out of the Prime Minister of Israel were discouraging to a great extent. He was challenging the public opinion in the Arab world, in the Moslem world and the Christian world," Mubarak said in Cairo.

"Violence and terrorism will never come to an end unless the peace process moves forward... unless the people feel or trust the progress in the peace process. I think it is detrimental to attend and listen and to agree with what Mr. Netanyahu says."
Mubarak also told Israel's Maariv newspaper that the Washington summit had not been prepared properly.

"I told (President) Clinton I believe preparations should have been made to ensure there would be some results from this summit, otherwise it serves no purpose," Mubarak told Israel's Maariv in an interview on Monday.
"I decided against going to Washington so as not to anger public opinion in my country which opposes the trip," he said.

Since his election in May on a platform that rejects the "land for peace" principle of a 1991 peace accord, Netanyahu has delayed redeploying Israeli troops from the West Bank town of Hebron -- which was scheduled for earlier this year.
Palestinians are also infuriated that final status talks, which include discussion of sticky issues like the statehood of Jerusalem, have been on hold since an inaugural session in May.
Analysts have described Mubarak's absence as a blow to the Washington summit, given Egypt's key position in the region and its hosting of two years of PLO-Israeli negotiations.

But Mubarak, whose country was the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, said he had faith in Clinton's ability to handle the situation and that Egypt was not skulking away from its role.
"Mr. Clinton is a very able man, he is a very sincere man I hope that he could succeed and I told him I am ready to help in any way but without being present," Mubarak said.
But he added: "What will they negotiate?...nowadays we must work on impelementing the previous agreements which have been signed with (former Israeli prime ministers) Mr. Rabin and Mr. Peres."
Mubarak told Maariv he spent more than two hours persuading a "despondent" Arafat to accept the summit invitation.
"Arafat trusts Clinton, but he doesn't trust you Israelis. The Americans are busy now with elections and you are taking advantage of this situation," the Egyptian leader said.

Calling on Netanyahu to implement the Israeli redeployment in Hebron, Mubarak said: "Fire is burning under the coals...He must do something, or you will be seen as liars and violence will erupt again."
The Egyptian president said he had given Netanyahu "one, two, three chances" and last urged him to take action on Hebron in a telephone conversation last Wednesday.
"I told him: Netanyahu, do something. Redeploy in Hebron so that people can see you are doing something. He did not respond but simply changed the subject."

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said the key to the summit's success lay in Netanyahu changing his hardline position and that the United States, which gives Israel billions of dollars annually in aid, would be the best one to presuade him.

"What's needed is that Netanyahu should move. This is the essence of the summit. If that's not possible, if U.S. policy will not move him and the prestige of the U.S. president will not move him, then what would our role be?" Moussa told the London-based newspaper al-Hayat.
